extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, editors, and anyone seeking guidance on clear English composition
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive style and composition rules for clear, concise, and correct written English, aimed at improving sentence/paragraph construction, word usage, punctuation, and overall style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding ’s
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding ’s (the general rule for possessives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ’s even when the noun ends in s: Charles's friend. Exceptions and special cases are discussed in examples in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a comma in a series (Oxford comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: red, white, and blue. This preserves clarity in lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off parenthetic expressions with commas so the sentence reads smoothly and the inserted material is clearly separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The answer, of course, is yes. Avoid losing the sentence’s main thread by failing to mark asides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing an independent clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before conjunctions (and, but, for, nor, etc.) when they introduce a second independent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: She smiled, and he laughed. If the second clause is not independent, the comma may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not join independent clauses with a comma (avoid comma splices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent clauses should not be joined merely with a comma; use a semicolon, conjunction with comma, or make separate sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: He came, he saw. Correct: He came; he saw. Or: He came, and he saw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not break sentences in two
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid breaking a single idea into two short sentences where a single sentence (or a semicolon) is clearer; maintain sentence unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clauses that belong together remain connected logically and syntactically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a colon to introduce particulars, appositives, amplifications, or illustrative quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon is appropriate before a list, an appositive that amplifies, or a quotation that illustrates the preceding clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: She had three wishes: health, wealth, and freedom. Use a colon only after an independent clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a dash for abrupt changes or long appositives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the dash to set off abrupt changes in thought or to introduce a long appositive or summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dashes can add emphasis or mark an abrupt turn—use sparingly to avoid choppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The number of the subject determines the number of the verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure subject–verb agreement: singular subject takes singular verb; plural subject takes plural verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for intervening phrases, collective nouns, or constructions that disguise the true subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the proper case of pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nominative, objective, and possessive pronoun forms correctly in their syntactic positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Between you and me (not between you and I). When in doubt, test the pronoun alone: 'It is I' vs 'It is me' depends on formality and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: A participial phrase at the beginning must refer to the grammatical subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dangling participles: a participial phrase must modify the sentence’s grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful. Correct: Walking down the street, I thought the trees looked beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a suitable design and hold to it
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on an overall plan or structure for a piece (design) and maintain unity and coherence throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear design helps readers follow argument or narrative; avoid wandering or mixing incompatible approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paragraph the unit of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the paragraph as the basic unit: each paragraph should have a topic, development, and adequate transition to the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a topic sentence when appropriate and develop the idea fully before moving on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the active voice over the passive for directness and clarity, except when passive is more suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active: The committee approved the proposal. Passive may be used when agent is unknown or unimportant: The proposal was approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put statements in positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: Express statements positively rather than by negativing their opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive form is more direct and forceful. Instead of 'not bad,' say 'good' where accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concrete and specific words to vague generalities to convey clear meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of 'things were moving,' say what moved: 'the wagon rolled.' Specific nouns and vivid verbs strengthen prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove words that do not add meaning; make every word tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous Strunk maxim. Revise to eliminate redundancy, padding, and empty qualifiers (e.g., 'in order to' → 'to').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not string many short, loosely connected sentences; vary sentence structure and tighten connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loose (right-branching) sentences can become monotonous; use periodic or balanced constructions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express coordinate ideas in similar form (parallelism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate grammatical elements (words, phrases, clauses) should be expressed in parallel form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: She likes reading, writing, and skiing (not 'to ski'). Parallelism helps readability and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Place modifiers next to the words they modify; avoid separating words that belong together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplaced modifiers create confusion: 'She nearly drove for six hours' (did she almost drive or did she drive almost six hours?).

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing a plot or argument, maintain consistent tense to avoid confusing the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose present or past and stick to it for clarity and smooth flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: End sentences or clauses with the words you most want to emphasize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end of a sentence carries emphasis; structure sentences so the important idea falls there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow conventional matters of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to established conventions for manuscript form: punctuation, capitalization, italics, headings, hyphenation, and similar formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book gives rules for matters such as titles, numerals, abbreviations, and manuscript formatting—follow conventions to aid readers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use orthodox spelling and standard usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer standard/canonical spellings and idioms rather than novel or nonstandard variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in spelling and usage aids reader comprehension; avoid idiosyncratic forms without reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and compound modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens to join compound modifiers before nouns to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a well-known actor (hyphen before 'actor'), but 'the actor is well known' (no hyphen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid words and expressions commonly misused
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use words and expressions incorrectly; prefer the correct idiom or meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book supplies an extensive list of commonly misused words and preferred alternatives (e.g., affect/effect, different from/not different than, comprise/include vs compose). Consult the list for specific pairings and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place yourself in the background
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should be unobtrusive; the reader’s experience and the subject matter should come forward, not the author’s mannerisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-conscious or attention-getting devices; let nouns and verbs carry the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in a way that comes naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose natural phrasing and rhythms rather than forced or affected constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sentences to flow from thought; contrived style interferes with communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from a suitable design; revise and rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan a piece before writing and be prepared to revise extensively; revision is essential to clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline, draft, and then revise to cut redundancies and tighten argument or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nouns and verbs rather than ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor strong nouns and verbs; avoid overreliance on adjectives and adverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lean prose is stronger: 'He strode' is better than 'He moved with great speed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overwrite
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive ornament, elaborate figures, or overwrought expressions that distract from meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrain rhetorical excesses; clarity and economy trump showy phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overstate
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exaggeration and hyperbole that can make writing seem untrustworthy or melodramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let accurate description and measured claims build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the use of qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use qualifiers (rather, very, little, pretty) sparingly; they often add little and weaken assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut qualifiers that do not change meaning or precision; prefer stronger nouns and verbs instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fancy words; prefer the plain variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use obscure or ornate words when simple, well‑understood words will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clarity over showiness. If you choose an uncommon word, be certain of its meaning and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the standard idiom to the offbeat
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established idioms and constructions unless you have a reason to depart from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel constructions can jar readers; standard usage smooths reading and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dialect unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use dialect, slang, or nonstandard speech forms unless they serve an essential literary or documentary purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialects can be hard to render convincingly and may distract or alienate readers if used gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures of speech sparingly and precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech enrich prose when apt, but overuse or mixed metaphors weaken writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metaphors and similes that illuminate; avoid mixing images or piling on multiple comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not explain too much
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust readers to infer what follows logically; avoid over-explaining obvious connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concision often improves clarity; do not belabor points the reader already understands.
